text: The disappearance is staged, and the search that follows is entirely sincere, which is where the trouble starts. A botanist and his wife have gone missing on purpose, to avoid a cousin — an Anglican bishop currently running a campaign against a kind of writing rather closer to the family than he knows. Carné, working in France in 1937, sets it in a Victorian London that owes more to French ideas of England than to England, leaving everyone free to be as starched and literal as the farce requires. Ninety-five minutes, and the machinery is the pleasure: one lie needs a second, the second needs a witness, the witness needs feeding and housing, and a private embarrassment becomes a public search the botanist cannot call off without explaining himself. The bishop investigates. Everybody stays impeccably polite, which is exactly what keeps it moving.

Nando Moriconi has never left Rome and has already decided he is American. The comedy runs on that one conviction for eighty-five minutes: a young man performing a nationality he has only ever received at a distance, and correcting the people around him on how things are properly done. Steno keeps the joke local. Nando's America is assembled out of rumour and worn in public, and his neighbourhood treats it the way neighbourhoods treat any loud enthusiasm — with patience, and the occasional correction. The film sits on 100 film italiani da salvare, a curious honour for a picture about wanting to be somewhere else, though the appetite in it is recognisable enough. What holds up is the tenderness underneath the mockery. Nando is absurd, and he is also the only person here with a plan.

Twelve years after the footage was shot, the man who shot it sat down and cut it again. Herbert G. Ponting carried a motion picture camera to Antarctica with Captain Scott's expedition, and the material first reached audiences in 1912 as With Captain Scott in the Antarctic. The 1924 version is his second pass at it: re-edited, re-issued, one hundred and eight minutes long. That gap is where the film gets interesting. Getting an image at all in that cold was a mechanical problem — the camera, the stock, the hands working both. Deciding a decade later what the expedition should look like to people who were never there is a different order of choice, and it is the one he made twice. Ice, animals, the labour of moving anything at all: he shot it in the field and then built it at the bench.

The butler arrives with better manners than the people paying him, and the household never recovers. A transport contractor has come suddenly into money; his wife has firm ideas about what money ought to look like from outside; Hyppolit is engaged to supply the difference. What he supplies is judgment. Meals change, clothes change, the hours of the day are rearranged, and the man who owns the business finds himself a guest in his own dining room. Seventy-two minutes, made in Hungary in 1931, when films there had just acquired voices and a comedy could be carried on tone alone — who is entitled to correct whom, and how courteously. Hungarian audiences have never let it go. It still plays there regularly, which is a longer life than most comedies are given.

The target is a system rather than a person, which is the harder thing for a comedy to keep in frame for ninety-four minutes. Luigi Zampa took the Italian health service as his subject in 1968 and a working doctor as his way in, and the method is accumulation rather than escalation — the same absurdity, in a slightly different office. Satire aimed at an institution has no villain available to punish and no reconciliation to arrange. It can only show the thing running. The doctor is the useful figure because he is inside the machinery and paid by it at once: his living arrives through the arrangement he is being asked to laugh at. The annoyance in the film is not disguised as anything else, and it is directed at an arrangement the audience knew from the inside.

The army stops being an army, and the men inside it start walking. Italy's surrender to the Allies scatters the units, and a chain of command becomes a great many private problems: a uniform that meant one thing yesterday, a house some distance off, and nobody left with the authority to say how to get there. Luigi Comencini takes 117 minutes over it and files the result as comedy, war and drama at once, which is honest, because a road produces all three. The pressure is concrete throughout — food, distance, whether the next village has heard the news, whether anyone will open a door to a man dressed like that. Going home turns out to be the first thing these men have ever done without orders, and none of them is practised at it.

Seventy-nine minutes, a waterfront lunch counter, and a policeman who keeps finding reasons to walk past it. Danny Dolan has a beat; Helen Riley has a job behind the counter; Raoul Walsh, in 1932, had no interest in slowing either of them down. The economy of it is the surprise. There is a plot and the film gets through the plot without ceremony, because what it actually cares about is two quick people enjoying the fact that the other one is quick. It carries a place on the 1001 Movies list, which for an American picture this short and this unbothered is a pleasing outcome. The docks supply weather, noise and a class position — these are people who work shifts — and the courtship is negotiated in the gaps between them.

A minister loses his office for drinking, and for preaching more daringly than his church would allow. What follows takes three and a half hours, and the length is not padding. Mauritz Stiller's 1924 film gives Gösta Berling a second position as a tutor in a countess's household, and the running time buys the slow accumulation of a social world — house by house, obligation by obligation — until a man with no standing of his own is composed entirely of other people's hospitality. He falls in love with the countess Marta's stepdaughter. Marta has arrangements of her own in view, and the film is patient enough to let both developments proceed at the pace of a Swedish winter. Drawing rooms, ice, and a charming man with nothing to trade but the charm.

Two kings, cousins and neighbours, share a border and a habit that neither of them can leave alone. The habit is gambling, and the young woman both of them want — Sunita, daughter of the hermit Kanwa — is the point where the habit stops being private. Franz Osten made this in 1929 as a German production carrying an Indian story and a Hindi title, Prapancha Pash, which is an odd and productive arrangement. Seventy-four minutes is a tight frame for two rulers, a hermit's household and appetites that outrun both kingdoms, and the compression shows in how much gets done by position — who stands where, who is watching, who is owed a favour and by whom. Two men who cannot govern an appetite of their own go on governing everyone else, and the film keeps that quietly in view.

The opera house has been rebuilt, and something inside it objects to the renovation. China, 1937: a horror film that also intends to be a musical and a romance, and spends 113 minutes declining to choose. Four genres are listed for it, and all four are load-bearing. The Phantom of the Opera is the source, relocated — Song Danping haunts the new theatre and its young star — and the charge comes from the collision of registers, songs delivered straight into a story that keeps darkening around them. Weibang Ma-Xu treats the building as a machine with a front and a back, an auditorium and everything the auditorium is not allowed to see, and the dread leaks between the two. The music is not relief from the horror. It is the same substance, sung from a stage.

First the fairground, then the wedding, then a French manager with a better offer. A modest Neapolitan man meets a young woman whose body draws crowds, and the film follows the small, entirely reasonable steps by which one person's life becomes another person's livelihood. The comedy is in the bookkeeping. Marco Ferreri keeps the tone level and lets the arrangements be discussed in plain commercial language — venues, terms, what a French contract might be worth — while the woman is present for every word of it. Ninety-two minutes, spoken in Italian and produced out of France, and not once raised to a shout. What the film is actually about is how easily affection and management become the same activity, and how long a marriage can run on the second while calling itself the first.

Four men take banks; one policeman is handed the job of finding them, and the film keeps both halves in view. Carlo Lizzani made it in 1968 and built it as a manhunt rather than a caper, which changes what the ninety-eight minutes are for: not the planning of a job but the arithmetic of pursuit — hours, distances, roads out, a city that is large but finite. Milan is the third party here, treated as a working place with traffic in it rather than a backdrop, with exits that lead somewhere specific. The four are violent and the film does not decorate that, or apologise for it. The detective's problem is not moral, it is logistical, and the two tracks tighten toward each other at a rate the audience can feel.

Piazza Navona, two families a staircase apart, and one young woman both boys have decided on. Salvatore and Romolo are broke, good-looking and inseparable, and in the Rome of 1957 that combination leaves them nowhere to put a secret. They live with their parents, which is less a fact about housing than a fact about how much room a young man has to be foolish in. Every move either one makes is watched by mothers, neighbours and each other, and the square works as a stage with permanent seating around it. Dino Risi keeps it at ninety-seven minutes and at eye level, and the pleasure is in watching a friendship absorb a strain it was never built for. Giovanna is not a prize to be awarded, whatever the two of them assume, and the film gets funnier every time it remembers that.

The request is simple enough to state in a sentence: an Italian man would like a few minutes with the Pope. Everything after that is corridors. Marco Ferreri's 1972 film takes the Vatican as an administrative body rather than a spiritual one — desks, referrals, courteous men whose work is to absorb a request without ever refusing it — and sets one stubborn petitioner against the building's talent for absorption. It runs 108 minutes and is filed as comedy and drama at once, which is accurate; the joke and the injury are the same event viewed from different distances. Nobody inside the institution is a monster. They are all performing their duties correctly, which is the difficulty, and the man wants a thing for which no procedure exists.
